# 13.3.3 The Subgroup Generated by a Set; Cyclic Subgroups

Given a group $G$ and a subset$S \subseteq G$, we can always ask: what is the smallest subgroup of$G$ that contains every element of$S$? Such a subgroup must exist, since the intersection of any collection of subgroups is itself a subgroup, and we can intersect all subgroups that contain$S$. The result is the **subgroup generated by$S$**, written$\langle S \rangle$. This construction is fundamental: it allows us to build subgroups from specified elements and to understand$G$ through the subgroups generated by its parts.

Concretely, $\langle S \rangle$ consists of all finite products of elements of$S$ and their inverses --- all "words" of the form$s_1^{\epsilon_1} s_2^{\epsilon_2} \cdots s_k^{\epsilon_k}$ where each$s_i \in S$ and each$\epsilon_i \in \{1, -1\}$. One verifies this set is a subgroup: the empty product gives the identity, products of such words are such words, and the inverse of$s_1^{\epsilon_1} \cdots s_k^{\epsilon_k}$ is$s_k^{-\epsilon_k} \cdots s_1^{-\epsilon_1}$. This description is both the most explicit and the most useful in practice. For example, in$S_3$ the subgroup generated by$\{(1\;2), (1\;3)\}$ is all of$S_3$, since composing these two transpositions produces a$3$-cycle, and together the transpositions and the$3$-cycle account for all six elements.

The most important special case is when $S = \{g\}$ consists of a single element. The **cyclic subgroup** generated by$g$ is
$$\langle g \rangle = \{g^n : n \in \mathbb{Z}\} = \{\ldots, g^{-2}, g^{-1}, e, g, g^2, \ldots\}.$$
It is the smallest subgroup containing $g$, and its size is exactly the order of$g$:$|\langle g \rangle| = \mathrm{ord}(g)$. In additive notation,$\langle g \rangle = \{ng : n \in \mathbb{Z}\}$; for instance,$\langle 2 \rangle$ in$(\mathbb{Z}, +)$ is the set of all even integers$2\mathbb{Z}$.

If $g$ has finite order$n$, then the distinct powers are$\{e, g, g^2, \ldots, g^{n-1}\}$ and$g^n = e$. Two powers$g^a$ and$g^b$ are equal iff$n \mid (a - b)$. If$g$ has infinite order, all powers$g^n$ for$n \in \mathbb{Z}$ are distinct. The cyclic subgroup$\langle g \rangle$ is isomorphic to$\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}$ in the finite case (order$n$) and to$\mathbb{Z}$ in the infinite case.

Cyclic subgroups are the atoms of group theory. Every element of every group generates a cyclic subgroup, and understanding the cyclic subgroups of $G$ --- their orders, their intersections, how they fit together --- is a primary strategy for analyzing the structure of$G$. When$G$ itself equals$\langle g \rangle$ for some element$g$, we say$G$ is a cyclic group, studied in depth in Section 13.4.

**Example 1.** In $S_4$, find$\langle (1\;2\;3), (2\;3\;4) \rangle$. We compute products to see what elements are generated. First,$(1\;2\;3)(2\;3\;4)$: apply$(2\;3\;4)$ first:$1\to 1$,$2\to 3$,$3\to 4$,$4\to 2$; then$(1\;2\;3)$:$1\to 2$,$3\to 1$,$4\to 4$,$2\to 3$; net:$1\to 1\to 2$,$2\to 3\to 1$,$3\to 4\to 4$,$4\to 2\to 3$, giving$(1\;2)(3\;4)$. Since$(1\;2)(3\;4)$ is a product of two disjoint transpositions (even), and$(1\;2\;3)$,$(2\;3\;4)$ are both$3$-cycles (even), all elements in the subgroup are even. In fact$\langle (1\;2\;3), (2\;3\;4) \rangle = A_4$, which can be verified by showing the generated subgroup has order$12$.

**Example 2.** Compute $\langle r^2 \rangle$ in$D_6$ (dihedral group of order$12$, with$r$ of order$6$). Since$r$ has order$6$,$r^2$ has order$6/\gcd(2,6) = 3$. So$\langle r^2 \rangle = \{e, r^2, r^4\}$, a cyclic subgroup of order$3$.

**Example 3.** In $\mathbb{Z}/12\mathbb{Z}$, find$\langle \bar{4} \rangle$. We compute multiples of$\bar{4}$:$\bar{4}, 2\bar{4} = \bar{8}, 3\bar{4} = \overline{12} = \bar{0}$. So$\langle \bar{4} \rangle = \{\bar{0}, \bar{4}, \bar{8}\}$, a subgroup of order$3$. The order of$\bar{4}$ is$3 = 12/\gcd(4, 12) = 12/4$, consistent with the formula$\mathrm{ord}(\bar{k}) = n/\gcd(k,n)$ in$\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}$.

**Example 4.** Show that $\langle (1\;2), (3\;4) \rangle$ in$S_4$ is isomorphic to$\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z} \times \mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}$. The elements generated are:$e$,$(1\;2)$,$(3\;4)$, and$(1\;2)(3\;4)$ (since$(1\;2)(3\;4) = (3\;4)(1\;2)$ because the cycles are disjoint). So$\langle (1\;2), (3\;4) \rangle = \{e, (1\;2), (3\;4), (1\;2)(3\;4)\}$, a group of order$4$. Every nonidentity element has order$2$, so this is the Klein four-group$V_4 \cong \mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z} \times \mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}$.

**Example 5.** In $GL_2(\mathbb{R})$, the subgroup$\langle A \rangle$ generated by$A = \begin{pmatrix}0 & -1 \\ 1 & 0\end{pmatrix}$ (rotation by$90°$). We compute:$A^2 = \begin{pmatrix}-1&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix}$,$A^3 = \begin{pmatrix}0&1\\-1&0\end{pmatrix}$,$A^4 = I$. So$\langle A \rangle = \{I, A, A^2, A^3\}$, a cyclic subgroup of order$4$ inside$O(2) \subset GL_2(\mathbb{R})$. This subgroup is isomorphic to$\mathbb{Z}/4\mathbb{Z}$ and corresponds geometrically to rotations by multiples of$90°$.
